data.title: Anton Petrovský-Šichman – fifty years since the death of the archaeologist of the Váh region
data.excerpt: When we were unveiling the information panel at the barrow cemetery in Visolaje, Mr Meliš reminded us that it was exactly fifty years since the death of Anton Petrovský-Šichman, the archaeologist who discovered dozens of hillforts, settlements and barrows in the Váh region. With the author’s permission we bring you in full the memorial article that Zuzana Staneková published in Slovenská archeológia LXV-1 (2017).
data.metaTitle: Anton Petrovský-Šichman – fifty years since his death
data.metaDescription: A remembrance of Anton Petrovský-Šichman, the archaeologist who discovered some 700 sites and laid the foundations of archaeology in the Žilina Basin.

mediaTexts.alt: A black-and-white portrait of a young man in a corduroy jacket

children.text: When we were unveiling the information panel at the barrow cemetery in Visolaje, Mr Meliš pointed out to me that it was exactly fifty years since the death of the eminent archaeologist Anton Petrovský-Šichman, with whom Meliš had worked very closely. I said to myself that I had to write at least a short article about it, so that we at hradiska.sk too could honour the memory of a man who discovered dozens of hillforts, settlements and barrows in the Váh region. To this day, however, I have not got round to it. I was all the more pleased when the new issue of Slovenská archeológia (LXV-1 of 2017) carried an article by the archaeologist Zuzana Staneková, written in remembrance of Šichman. With the author’s permission we therefore bring you this article in its full version.
Fifty years since the death of Anton Petrovský-Šichman

The name of Anton Petrovský-Šichman is linked with the beginnings of the Považie Museum in Žilina and with the rise of systematic archaeological work in the Žilina Basin. On 5 May 2017 we shall mark the fiftieth anniversary of his death.

Anton Petrovský-Šichman was born on 7 July 1919 in Žilina, the son of a shoemaker. After studying at the Realgymnasium in Žilina he attended the Pedagogical Academy, and once he had completed his higher studies he worked in the years 1938–1942 as a teacher at primary schools in Ďurčiná, Fačkov and Bánová. In 1943 he returned to the school bench once more, enrolling at the Faculty of Arts of the Slovak University in Bratislava, where he studied archaeology and linguistics. In 1949 he was awarded the degree of PhDr. Subsequently, in 1950, he began to work as an external collaborator of the then Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences and Arts. He remained in this position until 1957. He gave up his post, however, in order to join the Regional Museum in Žilina, where he became one of its first specialist staff (Považské múzeum 2012, 89). He held this post until his premature death on 5 May 1967. He died at the age of 47, not having lived to see his 48th birthday.

blocks.alt: Fifty years since the death of Anton Petrovský-Šichman

children.text: As a museum employee he spent most of his working time in the field. He built on the work of his teacher, Vojtech Budinský-Krička, who in the 1930s had intensively investigated northern Slovakia and who later took part in some of Šichman’s excavations as a consultant.

During his time in the post of archaeologist he discovered around 700 archaeological sites from various historical periods. Through lectures he sought to awaken an interest in history among pupils of primary and secondary schools. He even set up a club for young enthusiasts, whom he then took with him into the field as helpers. In this connection one cannot fail to mention Ondrej Šedo, who was the only member of the archaeological club to become a professional archaeologist. If we speak of the people by whom Petrovský-Šichman was surrounded during his time at the Považie Museum, it is also necessary to mention Gabriel Povala, a priest by origin and a man with a troubled fate in political terms

, who at one period of his life worked at the Považie Museum as an auxiliary “technician”, and who with his pragmatic thinking occasionally kept Petrovský-Šichman’s lofty notions down to earth (Moravčík 1998, 42).

Besides hundreds of field surveys, Anton Petrovský-Šichman carried out several archaeological excavations in the area of the former Žilina region, when its territory also included the districts of Považská Bystrica and Púchov. In addition to the activities that we now know as “excavations for research and documentation purposes”, he carried out site inspections and, where necessary, excavations of all digging and construction work in the area covered by the Považie Museum. Although he was drawn above all to the period of early medieval occupation, as a museum archaeologist he could not afford to devote himself exclusively to this period; on the contrary, he carried out excavations without distinction wherever they were needed or useful.
Among his activities at sites of the Lusatian culture, his most important excavations include the cemeteries at Jasenica-Chmelínec, Kotešová-Nivy, Sedmerovec-Niva and Gbeľany.

At Divinka, in the locality known as Ohrádza, he investigated a settlement of the Púchov culture. He regarded the uncovered settlement horizon as a multi-roomed dwelling house and later published this conclusion of his (Petrovský-Šichman 1966). At Mestečko, in the locality known as Skala, his excavation documented a hillfort of the Púchov culture

and the sacrificial site at Prosné, at that time the first documented in Slovakia, was also dated to this period; he investigated it at the end of his life together with J. Moravčík, then a fourth-year student at the Faculty of Arts of Comenius University in Bratislava. At Ilava he examined a cremation grave with Roman-period pottery. In 1957, at Považská Bystrica in the locality known as Dedovec, he discovered a Slavic settlement. He repeated the excavation of a Slavic settlement three years later at Prečín-Humenice, and finally, at Ivančiná in the locality known as Kratiny, he investigated a Slavic settlement in 1964.

In 1966 he carried out an archaeological excavation on today’s Mariánske námestie in Žilina, on the site of the planned town fountain, where, as J. Moravčík’s renewed excavation in 1995 confirmed, he discovered a high medieval settlement feature with a log construction and a wooden floor from the 14th–15th centuries (Moravčík 1970, 21; 2007, 18).
An important chapter in Šichman’s fieldwork were the Slavic barrow cemeteries. In 1956, at his instigation

, V. Budinský-Krička carried out an excavation of Slavic barrows at Žilina-Hôrky and Bitarová. In three phases (1958, 1959 and 1961) Petrovský-Šichman then continued the work at Bitarová, in the locality known as Kopence, investigating eleven of the total of 30 barrows identified, which formed part of a barrow cemetery covering approximately 200 x 70 m.

The excavation confirmed biritual burial at this cemetery, even though the skeletal remains had almost not survived owing to the acid soil there; its effect was also strongly apparent in the condition of the iron grave goods. In as many as eight barrows A. Petrovský-Šichman found an internal arrangement of the barrow graves in the form of rectangular wooden structures. The barrows at Bitarová were thus the first in Slovakia where this manner of burial was documented for the Early Middle Ages, and A. Petrovský-Šichman was the first archaeologist to put forward the assumption that they were a kind of “house of the dead”. He presented this conjecture as early as the commission meeting at the archaeological excavation at the barrow cemetery in Bitarová, where, however, it met with no support and some of those present even expressed the view that the area excavated was not a barrow but a settlement feature (Moravčík 1998, 26). In 1970 a contribution was published post mortem in which he again presented this conviction in the words: “It is probably a symbolic imitation of a burial chamber, whose ground plan represented a room.” (Petrovský-Šichman 1970, 202).

In 1960 Petrovský-Šichman investigated further barrows: three at Visolaje, in the locality known as Cesciny, and two at Krásno nad Kysucou; in 1962 two barrows at Bohunice, one at Sverepec and two at the barrow cemetery at Bánová, where in the case of barrow 1 he again discovered a wooden structure similar to that at Bitarová (Slaná 2013, 40). Today this theory of his about the dwelling of the dead is fully accepted and endorsed by the scholarly community.

He met with a minor failure in the investigation of barrows at Žilina, in the locality known as Chrasť, where, while still a student at the Faculty of Arts of Comenius University, he discovered three barrows, of which he also informed V. Budinský-Krička. Together they assumed that these might be “an early Slavic burial on the remains of an earlier occupation”

and, in an effort to verify this conjecture, A. Petrovský-Šichman undertook a trial excavation, yet he found no burial, only fragments of fired clay, a few sherds and pieces of charcoal. He informed Professor Budinský-Krička of the disappointing results of the excavation in a letter as well, which he ended with a contrite apology for his unfulfilled expectations in the words: “...Otherwise I very much regret that You were not entirely satisfied; I almost reproach myself for having dared to draw Your attention to Chrasť and to deprive You of time that You could have devoted to a more interesting feature. With complete respect, Yours devotedly A. J. Petrovský-Šichman”.

The correspondence of Petrovský-Šichman addressed to V. Budinský-Krička, which forms part of some of the files from the excavations he carried out, reflects his deep respect for his teacher, whom he often asked for advice or an opinion, especially in the early stages of his work in the field, and at the same time it is a reflection of his professional devotion and sense of responsibility.

Anton Petrovský-Šichman spent most of his working time in the field. He travelled to the sites by the only means of official transport that the Považie Museum had at its disposal at the time – a motorcycle. It soon became his hallmark, and thanks to it those who remember him recall him to this day. Despite his heavy workload in the field, he also sought to spread the insights he had gained during surveys and excavations. He published several specialist articles in various periodicals, but his contributions “Slovanské osídlenie severného Slovenska” (Slavic occupation of northern Slovakia) and “Severozápadné Slovensko v dobe laténskej a rímskej” (North-western Slovakia in the La Tène and Roman periods), which appeared in Vlastivedný zborník Považia 6 and 7 (Petrovský-Šichman 1964; 1965), are regarded as the most fundamental. These two extensive articles still carry weight today, and for the archaeology of north-western Slovakia and for the study of archaeological material from the territory of the upper Váh region they are fundamental works that cannot be overlooked. In the contribution “Severozápadné Slovensko v dobe laténskej a rímskej” he presented a list of 324 archaeological sites in the territory of the former Žilina region that were known to him at that time. Many he discovered himself or had his attention drawn to them, and he visited most of the sites in person.

In view of his training in linguistics, he often attempted to explain the origin of the names of villages, localities and field names, and he published these theories of his as well, for which, however, he earned from the scholarly community rather a smile than recognition.

The number of archaeological excavations that he managed to carry out as an employee of the Považie Museum in Žilina was above standard for that time. The extraordinarily detailed documentation from the archaeological excavations he directed, which has survived in the museum, is likewise astonishing. His workload in the field was, however, largely reflected in his museum work, which he did not manage to attend to on the scale that the emerging archaeological collection required. At the time of his death only 47 items were registered in the inventory book of the archaeological collection

and dozens of wooden crates full of finds remained unprocessed. Even today, half a century after his death, the archaeology depository of the Považie Museum in Žilina holds hundreds of unregistered finds from various archaeological sites of the former Žilina region. Several of them have in recent years been processed by students into diploma theses, with some works dealing with individual sites (Dedovec, Ivančiná-Kratiny, Jasenica-Chmelínec, Kotešová-Nivy) and others with micro-regional or regional occupation in various historical phases. Many more are still waiting to be processed.

Anton Petrovský-Šichman is an important figure of Slovak archaeology. He belongs to that generation of archaeologists which laid the foundations of this scholarly discipline. His work, begun so to speak on “a green field”, is of enormous significance above all in the area of the Žilina Basin, where he made a fundamental contribution to knowledge of the region, and to such an extent that in the 1950s the north-west of the country was among the best-explored territories in Slovakia.
Zuzana Staneková
